speaker: SPEAKER_00
transcript: On July 13, Ohio Lieutenant Governor John Houston announced the introduction of the Ohio Personal Privacy Act. The draft bill offers a comprehensive framework that follows other recent US state privacy laws, but perhaps follows that of Virginia's Consumer Data Protection Act most closely. The law applies to organizations doing business in Ohio or whose product or services target consumers in the state. Businesses with annual gross revenues exceeding $25 million, or process personal data of 100,000 or more Ohio consumers, or derive 50% of gross annual revenues from the sale of personal data would be covered. Like other laws, it does offer some consumer rights, including correction, deletion, and portability, as well as an opt-out right for the sale of personal data. Most notably, the OPPA includes a carve-out for businesses that reasonably conform to the US National Institute of Standards and Technologies' privacy framework. I recently caught up with Lieutenant Governor Houston to discuss the bill, the NIST to save harbor, and what the OPPA means for businesses and the future of privacy law at the state, federal, and international levels. As a caveat, we did experience some slight technical difficulties with the recording of Lieutenant Governor, who stood near the beginning of our conversation. I asked him why a privacy law now. He said there are not enough good protections for consumers and that businesses need to be able to innovate while being held to account for bad privacy practices. But compliance should be reasonable. We joined the conversation as Houston begins to discuss the NIST portion of the bill.
